question: When a parallel beam of light passes through a convex lens, after refraction it:

options.text: converges to a point on the principal axis
forms a virtual image at infinity

solution:
The correct answer is __**converges to a point on the principal axis**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• A **convex lens** is also known as a **converging lens** because of its ability to bring parallel rays of light together at a single point.
 
• When a beam of light consisting of rays **parallel to the principal axis** strikes the surface of a convex lens, the rays undergo **refraction** twice—once when entering the lens and once when exiting it.
 
• After passing through the lens, these refracted rays **converge** and intersect at a specific point on the **principal axis**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• This specific point where the parallel rays meet is called the **Principal Focus** (denoted by **F**). Since the rays actually meet at this point, the focus of a convex lens is considered a **real focus**.
 
• The **converging action** occurs because the lens is **thicker at the center** than at the edges, causing the light rays to bend more toward the thicker part of the glass.
